previous_versions.body: I think "risky" is too general of a term. I like how @elarlang is defining what it means and I think it's the right direction.
I think "risky" is too general of a term. How about "libraries with a history of security problems" or "libraries with poor security design" or similar? I think we should be more specific here.
I think risky is too general of a term. How about "libraries with a history of security problems" or "libraries with poor security design" or similar? I think we should be more specific here.
And 15.1.5 seems like too general of a requirement and I think we should consider removing it.
And 15.1.15 seems like too general of a requirement and I think we should consider removing it.

For 15.1.4 I would suggest just a little more clarity and some grammar cleanup:

_15.1.4 Verify that application documentation highlights “risky” third-party libraries, including those with missing or poorly implemented security controls, those that are poorly maintained, unsupported, or end-of-life, and those with a history of significant vulnerabilities._

For 15.1.4 I would suggest just a little more clarity and some grammar cleanup:

15.1.4 Verify that application documentation highlights “risky” third-party libraries, including those with missing or poorly implemented security controls, those that are poorly maintained, unsupported, or end-of-life, and those with a history of significant vulnerabilities.

Let me share my comments on discussion above:

- risky is the widely used term in security. And it used at start of V15.1 as a regular word without quotes. 
- agree that this term should be like "highlighted" and "focused to" specifics behind 15.1.4 and 15.1.5
- Really like @jmanico idea on complexity and business logic... But it seems more close to components/libraries with critical functionality. And maybe this directions is worth to put into separate requirement. 
- @elarlang, honestly, I have the same feeling that 15.1.5 more close to L2... 

Colleagues, could you please have a look at following wording (slightly changed what was suggested above, risky can be quoted, as you decide): 

in 15.1.4 -- it is about quality of implemented security controls
> Verify that application documentation highlights risky third-party libraries, which has missing or poorly implemented security controls. That should include libraries that are poorly maintained, unsupported, in the end of life, or that have historically significant vulnerabilities.

in 15.1.5 -- it is about high likelihood of being dangerously exploited 
> Verify that application documentation highlights parts of application which has high likelihood of being exploited using external untrusted data. Such operations should include deserialization of untrusted data, raw file parsing, or direct memory manipulation.

Regarding 15.3.10:
As for me, it is far from Defensive coding itself. But I can't find more suitable section. The other close section could be (V13.4 Build and Deploy)[https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x22-V13-Config.md#v134-build-and-deploy]. 
Some comments on requirement itself:
- **auto-update**: works well, when it is something close to end-user applications. But when it is servers applications, could be useless as company must have change management process... 
- **digital signing of updates**: could be more close to "build and deploy" section. And in 13.4 there are no requirements related to digital signing of components... 

Potentially part related to "updates must be digitally signed, with the digital signature being validated before installing or executing the update." can be moved to section 13.4. And part related to auto-update removed.

Colleagues, first of all -- a really not easy topics were touched... And unfortunately it really could be that to reach result that met all expectations may be difficult or even impossible.

Let me share my thoughts regarding 15.1.4, 15.1.5 :
1. Adding definitions really helps in understating of context and make requirements lighter and clearer. @tghosth, really like this idea!
2. When it comes to "dangerous functionality", as for me -- it works well. At least much better then we have. 
3. When it comes to "risky component", it seems we could confuse readers due to adding _**"or includes "dangerous functionality""**_.  This make scope of 15.1.5. **to be included** into scope of 15.1.4. And this brings us to the topic of differences between 15.1.4 and 15.1.5. As @jmanico suggested, should we highlight a root cause of "risky components" -- quality of implemented security controls. For example put "risky component" definition in following way:
> A "risky component" is one that has missing or poorly implemented security controls. For example components that are poorly maintained, unsupported, in the end-of-life, has a history of significant vulnerabilities.

4. I also left two minor comments on PR #2977 , but the most important topics are above.

Regarding 15.3.10 and 13.4.3 readers may not be aware on history behind these requirements and take them as is.
I could be wrong but, please look at these too requirements together.
> 15.3.10 Verify that, if the application has an auto-update feature, updates must be digitally signed, with the digital signature being validated before installing or executing the update.

> 13.4.3 Verify that application code or functionality can only be changed via the standard update or build process and not directly in production through application functionality or some other direct modification mechanism.

It could be that following questions raised:
1. How component could be auto-updated if it "can only be changed via the standard update or build process and not directly in production "?
2. When it comes to Web app: do actually digital signature is the only way that must be used for update validation? For example, couldn't SRI be used for checking integrity of WebApp scripts update? 

I support 13.4.3, as it reflects industry used practice.
But should we go with 15.3.10 in explanation and section we have now? 
@elarlang if possible, could you share a bit of history or link to behind 15.3.10?

It originates back to 2019, to v4.0 requirement 10.3.1, so I don't know the background and reasoning behind that. The understanding of the scope back then was different and this was my question at the moment - do we still consider it to be in the scope.
